meta.title: Who really said "You break it, you own it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Colin Powell's coinage. Thomas Friedman published "You break it, you own it" in the NYT on 12 Feb 2003 — and Powell said so himself: "Friedman did it."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You break it, you own it'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Colin Powell's coinage. Thomas Friedman put it in print on 12 Feb 2003, over an old shop-sign proverb — and Powell publicly gave the credit back.

answer.label: Not coined by Powell — Thomas L. Friedman's line
answer.authorDates: b. 1953 · American journalist & New York Times foreign-affairs columnist
answer.sourceLine: The exact wording is Friedman’s. His New York Times column of 12 February 2003, “Present at . . . What?” ↗, reads: “The first rule of any Iraq invasion is the pottery store rule: You break it, you own it.” Powell inherited the credit through Bob Woodward’s Plan of Attack (2004), which reports it as a label Powell and Richard Armitage used privately — and Powell handed the credit back, telling CNN in 2004 “it’s Tom Friedman’s fault” ↗. Friedman in turn was reworking an anonymous American shop-sign proverb documented since 1948.

source.heading: Where the wording is actually documented

docMeta.dd: The New York Times, op-ed column by Thomas L. Friedman
Shop sign, “If You Break it—You’ve Bought It!” — reported by Walter Winchell, 1948

source.excerpt: The first rule of any Iraq invasion is the pottery store rule: You break it, you own it. We break Iraq, we own Iraq — and we own the primary responsibility for rebuilding a country of 23 million people …
trail: 1948 — a shop sign, not a statesman. Walter Winchell’s syndicated column described a Greenwich Village bric-a-brac shop whose placard warned “If You Break it—You’ve Bought It!” Variants ran in gift shops through the 1950s and 1960s, per Barry Popik’s citation list ↗.

September 2002 — Friedman brings it to Iraq. On NPR’s Weekend Edition Saturday, 7 September 2002, he said: “I kind of have a Pottery Barn view of this issue … there’s a sign that always says, ‘Break it and you own it.’” He put the finished wording in print on 12 February 2003 — both transcribed by Popik ↗.

2004 — Woodward hands it to Powell. Plan of Attack, page 150, quotes Powell warning Bush “you are going to be the proud owner of 25 million people” and adds, in Woodward’s own voice: “Privately, Powell and Deputy Secretary of State Richard Armitage called this the Pottery Barn rule: You break it, you own it” — reproduced on Wikipedia ↗. That sentence is a report of a private label, not a transcript of Powell speaking.

2016 — Friedman claims it outright. “Yes I coined that phrase … I happened to see Powell and Armitage in their office at State a few days later and used it with them,” he told Poynter ↗, adding that Powell “rather enjoyed getting credit for it after a while.”
source.excerptNote: Note what the printed column actually says: pottery store rule, not Pottery Barn rule. Friedman has said he swapped in the brand name only in spoken remarks. The famous five words — “You break it, you own it” — are already exact here, months before Bob Woodward attached them to Powell.
source.rightsHolder: Thomas L. Friedman and The New York Times Company
source.rightsNote: The sentence quoted here first appeared in a New York Times op-ed column published 12 February 2003, so it is squarely in copyright and is excerpted above only in the short measure a provenance note requires. The much older shop-sign proverb it reworks (“If you break it, you’ve bought it,” in print by 1948) is anonymous folk wording with no identifiable rights holder — but that is not the wording on this page.

author.name: Thomas L. Friedman
author.kicker: The columnist who actually wrote it
author.heading: Thomas L. Friedman
author.metaLine: b. 1953 · American journalist & New York Times foreign-affairs columnist
author.bio: Friedman writes the New York Times foreign-affairs column and has won three Pulitzer Prizes, in 1983, 1988 and 2002. He first floated the pottery-shop analogy for Iraq on NPR’s Weekend Edition Saturday in September 2002 and put it in print the following February. He has been blunt about authorship — “yes I coined that phrase and not just in whisper. I wrote a column about it” — while admitting he wrote “pottery store rule” in the paper but said “Pottery Barn Rule” in speeches, because he was afraid the chain might sue the Times.

cite.sourceCitation: Thomas L. Friedman, "Present at . . . What?" The New York Times, February 12, 2003. Popularly credited to Colin Powell via Bob Woodward, Plan of Attack (New York: Simon & Schuster, 2004), 150, where the phrase is reported as a private label rather than transcribed speech; Powell publicly disclaimed the coinage.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘You break it, you own it’?” Last verified 17 Aug 2026.

copyAttribution: "You break it, you own it." — Thomas L. Friedman, "Present at . . . What?", The New York Times, February 12, 2003. Widely credited to Colin Powell after Bob Woodward's Plan of Attack (2004), p. 150, reported it as a private label used by Powell and Richard Armitage. Powell disclaimed the coinage: "It is said that I used the 'Pottery Barn rule.' I never did it; Friedman did it." The underlying shop-sign proverb — "If you break it, you've bought it" — is in print by 1948.

misattribution.heading: Four things everyone gets wrong about this one
misattribution.intro: Almost every element of the popular story is off — the speaker, the store, and, in the most-quoted version, the verb.

items.why: Powell publicly disowned it. Asked about it in 2004 he told CNN’s Larry King, “It came from Tom Friedman, the [New York Times] columnist. So, it’s Tom Friedman’s fault” ↗. In October 2007 he was firmer still: “It is said that I used the ‘Pottery Barn rule.’ I never did it; [Thomas] Friedman did it.”

The chain has never had a you-break-it-you-buy-it rule; like most large American retailers it writes breakage off as a loss. A spokesperson told the St. Petersburg Times, “This is very, very far from a policy of ours” ↗. Friedman has said he wrote “pottery store” in the column partly for fear the chain would sue.

The variant that reached the widest audience is not the original. In the first Bush–Kerry debate on 30 September 2004, John Kerry said: “Secretary of State Colin Powell told this president the Pottery Barn rule: If you break it, you fix it” ↗ — wrong verb, wrong author, on a debate stage.

Long before any of them, the thought was a hand-lettered warning over fragile merchandise: a Greenwich Village placard reported by Walter Winchell in 1948, a Boston antique shop and a Miami Beach gift shop in 1952, all catalogued by Barry Popik ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Powell did say something close, and said so himself — his version was “once you break it, you are going to own it.” But the five-word form the world quotes was printed by Thomas L. Friedman on 12 February 2003, over a shop-sign proverb older than the store it got named after, as Popik’s citation trail shows ↗.

context.heading: Why the credit moved
lead: Two separate things happened, and the retelling fused them. In the summer of 2002 Powell warned George W. Bush about the aftermath of invading Iraq — Woodward’s Plan of Attack renders that warning as “you are going to be the proud owner of 25 million people.” Separately, Friedman coined a memorable label for exactly that argument, on NPR in September 2002 and in print on 12 February 2003. When Woodward’s book appeared in 2004 it presented the label as Powell and Armitage’s private shorthand, and the label and the warning became one quotation.

From there it hardened fast. Within months a presidential debate had Powell as the author — with the verb changed to “fix.” The line was short, it was moral, it was about a war going badly, and it needed a soldier’s voice more than a columnist’s. Friedman’s own theory is unsentimental: “I suspect Powell rather enjoyed getting credit for it after a while, especially after Iraq went bad, so I got conveniently erased.”
detailsBody: A small tell that these are genuinely different utterances rather than one quotation: the population of Iraq changes with the speaker. Friedman’s February 2003 column says a country of 23 million people. Woodward’s Powell says 25 million. Powell’s own later recollection says 26 million. Three numbers, three separate sentences — not one line passed intact from man to man.

The chronology does not line up either, and both accounts can still be true, because they describe different events. Woodward places Powell’s warning to Bush in the summer of 2002; Friedman says he used the pottery line on Powell and Armitage at the State Department a few days after his column ran the following February. A warning delivered in 2002 could perfectly well acquire its nickname in 2003.
context.pull: It is said that I used the ‘Pottery Barn rule.’ I never did it; Friedman did it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Walter Winchell's 1948 column described a Greenwich Village shop placard reading "If You Break it—You've Bought It!"; Friedman said on NPR 7 Sept 2002 "there's a sign that always says, 'Break it and you own it'"; his NYT column "Present at . . . What?" of 12 Feb 2003 reads "The first rule of any Iraq invasion is the pottery store rule: You break it, you own it. We break Iraq, we own Iraq—and we own the primary responsibility for rebuilding a country of 23 million people..."; Woodward's Plan of Attack (2004) p.150 reads "'You are going to be the proud owner of 25 million people'... Privately, Powell and Deputy Secretary of State Richard Armitage called this the Pottery Barn rule: You break it, you own it."

Reproduces the Woodward Plan of Attack p.150 blockquote; records Kerry's 2004 debate line; and quotes Powell's denial, sourced to The Atlantic (October 2007): "It is said that I used the 'Pottery Barn rule.' I never did it; [Thomas] Friedman did it ... But what I did say ... [is that] once you break it, you are going to own it, and we're going to be responsible for 26 million people..."; also notes Friedman used "the pottery store rule" in a February 12, 2003 column.

Friedman told Poynter: "Jim, yes I coined that phrase and not just in whisper. I wrote a column about it" (Feb. 12, 2003); "I happened to see Powell and Armitage in their office at State a few days later and used it with them. Powell then went over to the White House and said it to Bush"; "I called it the pottery store rule in my column but the 'Pottery Barn Rule' in my speeches because I was afraid the Pottery Barn might sue the NYT!"; "I suspect Powell rather enjoyed getting credit for it after a while, especially after Iraq went bad, so I got conveniently erased."

Wikiquote's Colin Powell page lists "You break it, you own it." in its sourced 2000s section, cited to Bob Woodward's Plan of Attack (2004), noting Powell was a key source and was cautioning President Bush before the Iraq war. It is not placed in a Disputed or Misattributed section.

Dates "If you break it, you've bought it" to at least 1952, when a Miami Beach gift shop posted the message above fragile items; notes Powell's association with the term; and carries Pottery Barn's denial to the St. Petersburg Times: "This is very, very far from a policy of ours. In the rare instance that something is broken in the store, it's written off as a loss."

Official transcript of the first Bush–Kerry presidential debate, 30 September 2004, containing Kerry's words: "Secretary of State Colin Powell told this president the Pottery Barn rule: If you break it, you fix it."

Reports that Powell told CNN's Larry King in 2004: "It came from Tom Friedman, the [New York Times] columnist. So, it's Tom Friedman's fault," and that Friedman told William Safire "I made up the whole thing."
Thomas L. Friedman was born July 20, 1953; he is a New York Times columnist on foreign affairs and has won three Pulitzer Prizes (1983, 1988, 2002).
Colin Powell was born April 5, 1937 and died October 18, 2021; four-star general; Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff 1989–1993; Secretary of State 2001–2005.
